query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Using a modified feedstock with an enlarged particle size distribution (i.e. incorporating larger particles than the 15–45 μm range) will increase the deposition efficiency in thermal-spray processing, thereby overcoming the coating thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and maintaining low as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock exhibiting insufficient thickness.
generation.intervention: Replace the standard 15–45 μm feedstock with a feedstock that includes a controlled fraction of larger particles (e.g., extending the upper limit to approximately 70 μm) while maintaining a similar overall composition.
generation.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition conditions typical for TBC bond coats with subsequent service in high-temperature environments, ensuring that process parameters (e.g., gas flow, temperature, standoff distance) remain constant except for the feedstock modification.
generation.structural_mediator: The increased particle mass and momentum from larger particles will enhance in-flight kinetic energy and melting behavior, leading to improved splat formation and stronger intersplat bonding, while the reduced relative specific surface area minimizes oxidation during flight.
generation.mechanism: Larger particles require less relative heating to reach full melting and deposit with higher momentum, resulting in a denser, thicker coating with lower susceptibility to oxidation because of shorter residence time at high temperatures relative to their volume.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified powder will yield a coating with a significantly increased thickness beyond that achieved with the 15–45 μm feedstock baseline, without compromising the microstructural integrity or increasing the degree of as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.baseline: Coating produced using 15–45 μm feedstock that does not meet the required thickness standard.
generation.boundary: The intervention remains effective under the same thermal-spray processing conditions and service temperatures typical for thermal barrier coating bond coats; it may not be effective if other process parameters are significantly altered or if oxidation control measures fail in alternative environments.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimal proportion of larger particles to include such that deposition efficiency is maximized without adversely affecting other coating properties. Additionally, the effect of larger particles on microstructural features under varying operational conditions needs confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a comparative experiment in which two sets of thermal-sprayed bond coats are deposited: one using the standard 15–45 μm feedstock (baseline) and the other using the modified feedstock with an extended upper size limit (e.g., 15–70 μm). All other processing conditions and parameters are kept constant. After deposition, evaluate coating thickness, microstructure (via SEM analysis), and oxidation levels (via EDS or XPS).
measurements: Microstructural integrity (splat bonding quality, porosity, and grain size via SEM)
Oxidation level (surface and bulk oxide content using EDS/XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified feedstock does not result in a statistically significant increase in coating thickness compared to the baseline, or if it leads to degraded coating microstructure (e.g., increased porosity or poor splat cohesion) or higher levels of as-sprayed oxidation, then the hypothesis is falsified.
